sources.news_title: Supreme Court Rejects Accused 9/11 Mastermind’s Bid to Dodge Death Penalty
sources.text:
by Fred Lucas
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged mastermind behind the 9/11 terrorist attacks, will again face the potential for the death penalty after the Supreme Court denied his appeal Monday.
Justices rejected Mohammed’s bid to reinstate a plea agreement that allowed him and two co-defendants who helped plot the attack to avoid the death penalty. Mohammed (pictured above) and the co-defendants are scheduled to stand trial before a military court beginning June 5, 2028.
The Supreme Court’s order Monday doesn’t explain why the appeal was rejected. Justice Brett Kavanaugh—who served in the George W. Bush administration’s Justice Department and assisted with terrorist prosecutions after 9/11—recused himself from reviewing the case.
The co-defendants have been held at the military prison at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, since 2006 and were charged in 2008 for their alleged roles in 9/11, when hijacked planes destroyed the World Trade Center and struck the Pentagon.
In July 2024, the Biden Defense Department announced that military prosecutors had reached a plea deal with Mohammed and alleged 9/11 co-conspirators Walid Muhammad Salih Mubarak bin ’Attash and Mustafa Ahmed Adam al Hawsawi that would remove the death penalty from consideration. However, President Joe Biden’s defense secretary, Lloyd Austin, canceled the plea agreement.
The three co-defendants appealed that decision, and a military court sided with them. However, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Austin.
Justices on Monday announced action in several other cases that could be considered in the current term.
Justices will hear arguments about racial preference for a Maryland magnet school program in the case of Association for Education Fairness v. Montgomery County Board of Education.
Justices will also hear a case on the constitutionality of an 1868 federal law that taxes distilled spirits but also bans home distilleries, in Department of Justice v. McNutt. Penalties could amount to $10,000 or five years in prison.
In the immigration case of Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, the high court invited the solicitor general to file a brief expressing the views of the federal government.
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird is defending a law that creates a state-level crime related to illegal reentry into the United States. Challengers contend Iowa can’t enforce its own immigration-related criminal laws when immigration enforcement is primarily a federal responsibility.
The questions raised by the petition include whether a plaintiff has standing to make a pre-enforcement challenge to the constitutionality of a statute and whether overlap between state and federal criminal immigration laws is enough to preempt a state law if enforcement could sometimes conflict with federal officials’ prosecutorial discretion.
In O’Donnell v. City of Chicago, the justices will decide whether the Windy City’s policy of impounding and selling a driver’s vehicle after two unpaid parking tickets, and extending that policy to other vehicles registered to the driver, including those never ticketed, is an unconstitutional seizure. The court will also consider whether the Constitution’s takings clause places any limit on the ability of a local government to confiscate property under its police power.
The high court on Monday denied the petition to hear a case from Gwynne Wilcox, who sued the Trump administration over her removal from the National Labor Relations Board. This could signal that the high court has moved on from the question of a president’s authority to remove members of executive branch boards and commissions. Justices previously cleared the way for Trump to oust a commissioner on the Federal Trade Commission.
– – –
Fred Lucas is senior investigative reporter for the Daily Signal. He is the author of “The Myth of Voter Suppression: The Left’s Assault on Clean Elections.”

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Blocks 9/11 Plea Deal Revival as Alleged Mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed Faces Death Penalty Risk
sources.text:
Supreme Court Blocks 9/11 Plea Deal Revival as Alleged Mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed Faces Death Penalty Risk
The ruling keeps the death penalty in play as four defendants face a provisional trial date of 5 June 2028 at Guantánamo Bay
The US Supreme Court on Monday rejected a bid to revive plea agreements that would have spared Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged mastermind of the 11 September 2001 attacks, and two co-defendants the death penalty, leaving the government free to pursue capital charges in a case that has remained unresolved for more than two decades.
The unsigned order leaves intact a July 2025 ruling by a federal appeals court upholding former US defence secretary Lloyd Austin's decision to cancel the agreements in August 2024. The deals would have required the three men to plead guilty in exchange for the government agreeing not to seek their execution. The justices did not explain declining to hear the appeal. Justice Brett Kavanaugh took no part in the decision.
Court Upholds Austin's Authority to Cancel Deals
The agreements were accepted on 31 July 2024 by Susan Escallier, a retired US Army brigadier general who served as the convening authority overseeing military commissions at Guantánamo Bay, the US naval base in Cuba where terrorism suspects have been detained since 2002. On 2 August 2024, Austin, who served as defence secretary under President Joe Biden, withdrew the government from the deals.
The cancellation triggered a dispute over who had the authority to approve the agreements. Military judges initially ruled that Austin could not reverse them, allowing proceedings to move towards the entry of guilty pleas. The government challenged those decisions before the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, a civilian federal appeals court.
In a 2-1 decision on 11 July 2025, the appeals court ruled that Austin had the legal authority to withdraw from the agreements. The majority found that the defendants had not begun performing the obligations set out in the deals before Austin intervened. The Trump administration continued to defend the cancellation, and the Supreme Court's refusal to hear the appeal leaves that ruling in force.
Four Defendants Face Provisional 2028 Trial Date
The capital case involves four men: Mohammed, Walid bin Attash, Mustafa al-Hawsawi and Ali Abdul Aziz Ali, also known as Ammar al-Baluchi. The plea agreements covered only the first three; al-Baluchi did not join the deals. All four face charges connected to the attacks, which killed 2,977 people when hijacked planes struck the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, while a fourth aircraft crashed in Pennsylvania.
Air Force Lt Col Michael Schrama, the military judge, set 5 June 2028 as the provisional start date for the trial at Guantánamo Bay on 26 August, rejecting prosecutors' proposal of January 2027. The timetable remains uncertain because disputes over evidence gathered during earlier CIA interrogations continue to complicate the proceedings. The judge ruled that prosecutors could not use an alleged confession Mohammed made to the FBI in 2007, finding it tainted by his treatment in CIA custody, including waterboarding. The government decided not to appeal.
The proceedings have been delayed by litigation over the military commissions' authority, the treatment of detainees and the admissibility of evidence. The Supreme Court's order resolves the latest challenge to the plea agreements, but it does not settle those separate questions or determine the defendants' guilt.
Plea Agreements Divided 9/11 Victims' Families
The proposed deals divided relatives of those killed in the attacks. Some opposed a negotiated resolution and wanted the defendants to face trial, with the possibility of death sentences. Others backed the agreements as a route to guilty pleas, public admissions and answers about the attacks after years of pretrial proceedings.
September 11th Families for Peaceful Tomorrows, an organisation of relatives of victims that advocates non-violent approaches to conflict, urged the Supreme Court to hear the appeal. The group supported restoring the agreements, which would have required the defendants to admit their guilt and accept life sentences. The arrangements also offered a framework for victims' relatives to address the men during sentencing proceedings.
The charges were brought in 2012, and the case has yet to reach a full trial. Steve Vladeck, a Georgetown law professor who filed a friend-of-the-court brief urging the justices to take the case, said the denial paves the way for the ongoing pretrial process, but described the 2028 trial date as unrealistic given the number of unresolved issues, according to CNN.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Blocks KSM 9/11 Plea Deal Restoration
sources.text:
The Supreme Court refused Khalid Sheikh Mohammed’s bid to restore a 2024 plea deal that would have spared the Sept. 11 mastermind the death penalty.
In Washington on Monday, the justices turned away the effort by the man long identified as the principal architect of the Sept. 11, 2001, terror attacks, with no noted dissents. Justice Brett Kavanaugh recused himself from the matter.
The decision leaves in place the cancellation of a controversial agreement that would have let Mohammed plead guilty and serve life without parole instead of facing capital punishment. His military trial is now set to begin June 5, 2028, at the U.S. naval base in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, where he has been held for more than two decades.
The New York Post reported the high court rejection of Mohammed’s push to revive the deal reached with the Office of Military Commissions.
Mohammed faces 2,977 counts of murder, terrorism, and violations of the law of war, among other charges. Those figures match the number of people killed when hijacked planes struck the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and a field in Shanksville, Pa.
On July 31, 2024, Mohammed and two co-defendants, Walid bin Attash and Mustafa al-Hawsawi, reached an agreement with the Office of Military Commissions. They would plead guilty and accept life sentences without the possibility of parole.
Two days later, then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin rescinded the agreement. Austin said only the Pentagon chief could authorize such a deal. The move came amid a national outcry over sparing the death penalty for the accused 9/11 plotters.
A divided panel of the D.C. appeals court upheld Austin’s action last year. Mohammed then sought Supreme Court intervention to put the plea back in force. The justices declined.
Kavanaugh sat out the case. He had served in the George W. Bush White House counsel’s office at the time of Mohammed’s capture in 2003.
A bipartisan commission report published in 2004 described Mohammed as the “principal architect of the 9/11 attacks.” He and four other accused men were first charged in 2008 and recharged four years later.
At a 2007 U.S. military hearing, Mohammed left little doubt about his role.
He told the hearing:
"I was responsible for the 9/11 operation, from A to Z,"
In the same setting he claimed he was “very sorry” children were killed in the attack and insisted, “I don’t like to kill people.”
Those words sit beside the scale of the plot. Nearly 3,000 people died in a single morning. Families have waited through almost 25 years of delay for a trial on the merits.
As recently as August, a military judge threw out statements Mohammed made about the attacks to the FBI in 2007. The judge ruled those statements were not voluntarily given. The FBI obtained them four years after his 2003 capture.
The CIA had conducted so-called “enhanced interrogation” sessions in the years after the attacks. Defense challenges to the reliability and voluntariness of later statements have repeatedly slowed the case.
Even with those rulings, the core charges remain. Mohammed still stands accused of murder on a mass scale, terrorism, and law-of-war violations tied directly to the deaths of 2,977 people.
With the plea deal off the table and the Supreme Court unwilling to revive it, the military commission process moves forward. Proceedings are scheduled to open June 5, 2028, at Guantanamo Bay.
Mohammed has already spent more than twenty years in detention there. The victims’ families have spent the same stretch without a full public reckoning in court.
Austin’s rescission kept the death penalty available. The D.C. appeals court left that decision intact. The Supreme Court’s refusal to intervene does the same. The case now returns to the path of a contested military trial rather than a negotiated life sentence.
Accountability for the worst terrorist attack on American soil was never supposed to turn on a quiet plea that erased capital consequences. The high court left that principle standing.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court Leaves Death Penalty on Table for Accused 9/11 Mastermind After Rejecting Plea Deal Appeal
sources.text:
The Supreme Court declined to reinstate agreements that would have spared Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two co-defendants from execution, allowing the long-delayed military prosecution over the September 11 terrorist attacks to proceed toward trial in 2028.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday, Oct. 19, rejected an appeal seeking to restore plea agreements for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged mastermind of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, leaving him and two co-defendants facing the possibility of capital punishment.
The decision preserves former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin’s 2024 cancellation of agreements that would have allowed the defendants to plead guilty in exchange for life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.
The Supreme Court’s order in Khalid Shaikh Mohammad v. United States denied the defendants’ petition without an explanation. Justice Brett Kavanaugh did not participate in the decision.
The ruling leaves intact a divided federal appeals court decision recognizing Austin’s authority to withdraw the agreements before they were implemented.
Mohammed and co-defendants Walid bin Attash and Mustafa al Hawsawi have spent years at the U.S. military detention facility at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, awaiting resolution of charges related to the terrorist attacks.
Mohammed is accused of helping devise and direct the plot in which 19 al-Qaida terrorists hijacked four commercial aircraft on Sept. 11, 2001.
Two planes struck the World Trade Center towers in New York City, while a third crashed into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia. The fourth aircraft crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers attempted to regain control from the hijackers.
Nearly 3,000 people were killed in the attacks, which prompted the United States to launch a global campaign against al-Qaida and its associated organizations.
The plea agreements were negotiated in 2024 between military prosecutors and defense attorneys after years of delays in the Guantanamo military commission proceedings.
Under the arrangements, Mohammed and the two other defendants would have admitted guilt in exchange for sentences of life imprisonment without parole.
The deals were approved by Susan Escallier, the Pentagon official responsible for overseeing military commissions at Guantanamo Bay.
However, Austin intervened shortly afterward, withdrawing her authority to approve the agreements and canceling them.
Austin maintained that decisions involving the potential death penalty in a case of such national significance should remain with the defense secretary rather than be delegated to another Pentagon official.
His intervention created a legal dispute over whether the agreements had already become binding before he attempted to revoke them.
Defense attorneys argued that the Pentagon had completed the necessary approval process and that Austin lacked authority to nullify the agreements retroactively.
A military judge initially agreed with the defense, allowing the plea arrangements to proceed.
A military appeals court subsequently upheld that determination, but the federal government challenged the rulings before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.
In July 2025, a divided three-judge panel ruled 2-1 that Austin had acted within his legal authority.
The majority concluded that the defense secretary retained the power to withdraw authorization for the agreements before the defendants formally entered their guilty pleas.
The dissenting judge disagreed, arguing that the government had failed to establish sufficient legal grounds for canceling the arrangements after they had been approved.
The Supreme Court’s refusal to review the case leaves the appeals court ruling in place but does not constitute a separate decision on the merits of the underlying legal dispute. <Cite refs={[“turn201814search19″,”turn201814news35”]}/>
The development represents another major turn in a prosecution that has faced more than two decades of legal complications.
Mohammed was captured in Pakistan in 2003 and initially held in the CIA’s secret detention program before being transferred to Guantanamo Bay in 2006.
His treatment while in CIA custody, including waterboarding and other coercive interrogation techniques, has remained a central issue in the criminal proceedings.
Defense lawyers have challenged the admissibility of statements obtained during or following interrogations, arguing that torture and mistreatment contaminated potential evidence.
Those disputes, combined with questions concerning classified information, military commission procedures and the defendants’ constitutional rights, have contributed to repeated delays.
The canceled plea agreements had been intended to resolve the prosecution without the complications of a lengthy capital trial.
However, relatives of the September 11 victims have remained divided over whether accepting guilty pleas would provide an appropriate conclusion.
Some families supported the agreements, arguing that life sentences and admissions of responsibility would provide greater certainty than continued litigation.
Others opposed removing the possibility of execution and maintained that a full trial was necessary to determine responsibility and deliver justice.
The differing views reflect the emotional and legal difficulties surrounding a case that has remained unresolved for a quarter-century.
According to Associated Press reporting, the three defendants are now scheduled to face trial before a military commission in 2028. <Cite ref=”turn201814news36″/>
The proceedings are currently scheduled to begin June 5, 2028, more than 26 years after the attacks.
A trial could involve extensive testimony, classified evidence and renewed disputes over the government’s treatment of detainees.
Prosecutors would be required to establish each defendant’s guilt under the applicable military commission rules, while defense attorneys would retain the ability to challenge evidence and raise procedural objections.
The possibility of capital punishment also means that sentencing could become a separate and lengthy stage if the defendants are convicted.
Monday’s decision does not establish the defendants’ guilt or determine their eventual sentences. It instead removes the immediate possibility of enforcing the previously negotiated plea agreements through the Supreme Court appeal.
For the families of September 11 victims, the ruling means that a final resolution remains years away.
The government will now continue preparing for a military trial involving one of the most consequential terrorism prosecutions in American history, with the death penalty remaining a potential outcome.

sources.news_title: US Supreme Court Rejects Bid to Revive Accused 9/11 Mastermind’s Plea Deal
sources.text:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Oct. 19 rejected a bid from the accused Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attack mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two other alleged plotters to hold the government to a plea deal that it had withdrawn.
The court wrote in its orders list released on the morning of Oct. 19 that the petition was denied. It did not give further explanation other than stating that Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh had not participated in the decision.
Mohammed has long been accused of spearheading and organizing the plot to crash hijacked passenger jetliners into New York City’s World Trade Center towers, the Pentagon building in Virginia, and a plane that crashed into a field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania.
“I have determined that, in light of the significance of the decision to enter into pre-trial agreements with the accused in the above-referenced case, responsibility for such a decision should rest with me as the superior convening authority under the Military Commissions Act of 2009,” Austin wrote in a memorandum issued in August 2024 and directed to Susan Escallier, a former convening authority for military commissions.
“Effective immediately, I hereby withdraw your authority in the above-referenced case to enter into a pre-trial agreement and reserve such authority to myself.”
The other men who made an appeal to the Supreme Court, alongside Mohammed, were Mustafa Ahmed al-Hawsawi and Walid bin Attash. All three are being held at the Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, military base.
In the Oct. 19 decision, the justices turned away appeals by the three who had also signed plea agreements in a lower court’s ruling that upheld Austin’s decision to void their deals.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit had rejected an argument that Austin, who served under former President Joe Biden, had acted too late.
The Supreme Court’s action marks the latest milestone in a military prosecution of the detainees that has been beset by two decades of legal gridlock. In August, a U.S. Air Force judge set the trial for Mohammed and his co-defendants for June 2028.
Mohammed remains the most well-known figure at the Guantánamo detention facility, which was established in 2002 by then-President George W. Bush to house foreign terrorism suspects in the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks that killed nearly 3,000 people.
Defense attorneys for Mohammed, including lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union, urged the Supreme Court to hear the case. They said Austin’s action in 2024 violated controlling military law and “prolonged the best chance for finality in the September 11 case in a quarter century.”
“Our country is now approaching the 25th anniversary of September 11, 2001. Pretrial proceedings in this case began in 2008 and the panel’s decision leaves no end in sight,” the lawyers wrote in their 336-page petition to the high court.
“The proceedings before the D.C. Circuit added another year of delay and created a tangle of residual legal issues that promise to further delay the possibility of a trial until well into the next decade.”

sources.news_title: The Legal Proceedings Against Khalid Sheikh Mohammed Have Become an Extended Farce
sources.text:
Because of Dick Cheney’s sweet tooth for torturing people and the eagerness of his underlings to satisfy it, the legal proceedings against Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the alleged “mastermind” of the 9/11 attacks, have become an extended farce. KSM has been imprisoned at Guantánamo for 20 years. Now they’re saying he will go on trial before a military commission ... two years from now. What a mess this has turned out to be.
In 2024, KSM and two other suspects struck a deal with the military authorities by which the death penalty would be taken off the table. Then Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin squashed that arrangement. A military court ruled that Austin did not have the right to do so, but a civilian court reversed that decision, so the three suspects appealed that ruling to the Supreme Court, which this week ruled in favor of the government. This allows the government to keep the death penalty on the table for KSM and his two fellow defendants.
So much of this protracted exercise was directly tied to the fact that the Bush administration made this a country that tortured people. In August, a judge ruled that, in any future proceeding, the government cannot use the transcripts of FBI interrogations of KSM. From PBS:
In late August, the U.S. military judge who set a June 5, 2028, trial date for Mohammed and three others charged in the September 11 attacks ruled that prosecutors could not use an alleged confession he made to the FBI in 2007. Those statements were deemed tainted because Mohammed was subjected to “enhanced interrogation techniques” overseas, including the simulated drowning technique called waterboarding. While the ruling was a blow to the prosecution, the U.S. government decided not to appeal, in part because doing so could have further delayed a possible trial.
We also can blame cowardly Republican politicians, especially the late Senator Lindsey Graham, for resisting any plan to try KSM in an American civilian courtroom.
For a time in 2009, it seemed Mohammed was headed to New York after then-Attorney General Eric Holder announced plans to try him and four other men charged in the September 11 attacks in a Manhattan courthouse just blocks from the World Trade Center site. Then-President Barack Obama, who had pledged to close the Guantanamo detention center, said Mohammed would face “the most exacting demands of justice.”

Others cited security concerns, saying it could again make New York a terrorist target. Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani, a Republican, called the plan unwise and said it showed “a lack of concern for the rights of the public.” Plans for a civilian trial were dropped.
David Raskin, a Washington lawyer now in private practice who would have led the government’s prosecution of Mohammed in New York if it hadn’t been abandoned, said in an essay published in The Washington Post on Wednesday that he is confident a civilian trial would have ended with a conviction. The military commissions, on the other hand, “became a defense lawyer’s dream,” beset by “endless litigation over their legality and procedures. ... I predict there will never be a completed military commission trial for Mohammed and the other September 11 defendants,” he said.

sources.text:
Supreme Court turns away appeal from alleged 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed
Washington — The Supreme Court on Monday rebuffed a bid from accused Sept. 11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two alleged accomplices to revive plea agreements that they reached with military prosecutors before being revoked by the Biden administration.
In an unsigned order, the high court turned away the appeals from Mohammed, Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid bin 'Atash of a lower court decision that prevented a military judge from enforcing pretrial agreements they reached with military prosecutors in 2024, which were withdrawn by then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin.
In rejecting their case, the government's withdrawal of the plea deals remains in place. Justice Brett Kavanaugh did not participate in the court's consideration of the appeal.
Mohammed, Hawsawi and bin 'Atash, were captured in 2003 and charged before a military commission with several crimes for their alleged roles in crafting and perpetrating the Sept. 11 attacks, five of which carry the death penalty. In August, the judge overseeing their cases set a trial date of June 2028, which depends on the parties meeting certain deadlines and milestones on time.
The prosecutions have been mired in lengthy legal delays over whether evidence extracted during their interrogations could be used in court. The defendants were held at secret CIA prisons, where they were subjected to "enhanced interrogation techniques," or torture, before they were moved to Guantanamo Bay in 2006. They were formally charged in 2008.
In 2023, following the appointment of retired Brigadier General Susan Escallier as the Convening Authority for military commissions, military lawyers began discussing plea deals with the defendants. Agreements were subsequently reached in 2024 and approved by Escallier, who oversees the military court at Guantanamo Bay.
Under the terms of the deals, the defendants would plead guilty to all charges arising from their alleged roles in the 9/11 terror attacks and serve life sentences, avoiding the death penalty. But shortly after the agreements were announced, Austin said he was revoking them.
But a military judge ruled in November 2024 that Austin's nullification of the deals was unlawful, rendering the agreements valid and enforceable. A military appeals court then said Austin couldn't rescind the plea deals because the defendants had begun to perform one of the terms.
The Justice Department then asked the D.C. Circuit to step in and find that Austin validly withdrew from the pretrial agreements. The D.C. Circuit sided with the government in a decision last year and ruled that the defense secretary "indisputably" had the authority to withdraw from the plea deals.
"The Secretary acted within the bounds of his legal authority, and we decline to second-guess his judgment," the D.C. Circuit panel found.

sources.news_title: Justices refuse to take on plea deal for 9/11 perpetrators
sources.text:
(CN) — The Supreme Court declined Monday to weigh in on the disposal of controversial plea agreements that could have provided closure to the long-delayed death penalty trial against two perpetrators of the 9/11 attacks.
Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the man accused of plotting the attacks, and one of his co-conspirators, Mustafa al Hawsawi, sought to enter guilty pleas under a deal that would have spared them the death penalty.
Almost two decades into their prosecution and captivity in Guantanamo Bay, the plea agreements were viewed by victims, the defendants and prosecutors as a way to bring closure to the case after it was derailed by the government’s now-infamous torture program.
But former Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin tried to withdraw the agreements; the D.C. Circuit overturned two military courts that found the withdrawal unlawful.
The justices did not explain their reasoning for denying the petition but noted Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a Donald Trump appointee, took no part in the decision.
The government opposed the Supreme Court’s review, arguing the D.C. Circuit ensured that political appointees get to decide whether Mohammed and al Hawsawi should face the death penalty.
Mohammed, also known as KSM, was named the principal architect of the Sept. 11 attacks in a 2004 report by the 9/11 Commission. He and al Hawsawi were detained in 2003 and held in secret CIA prisons, where they were tortured, until being transferred to Guantanamo Bay in 2006.
Prosecutors aren’t able to use confessions obtained during the CIA interrogations because the government used torture — including 183 rounds of waterboarding. During subsequent interrogations in 2007 at Guantanamo, Mohammed also confessed to his role in the attacks.
But earlier this year, a military judge also ruled the 2007 confessions — described as crucial evidence in the government’s case — couldn’t be used against Mohammed at trial. The blow to prosecutors’ case could further delay a potential trial, scheduled for June 2028.
Several Sept. 11 victim groups filed an amicus brief in support of Mohammed and al Hawsawi’s appeal. The victims argued the plea agreements, while imperfect, were a crucial step in holding the men responsible. They argued the D.C. Circuit’s ruling deprived them of closure.
Mohammed and al Hawsawi’s attorney could not immediately be reached for comment.
Sotomayor questions Chicago impoundment scheme
In a separate denial, Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote that a challenge to Chicago’s ability to seize a vehicle over as few as two unpaid parking tickets needs further litigation.
Justice Neil Gorsuch, a Donald Trump appointee, joined her statement.
Sotomayor noted lower courts are divided over how far police can go in taking property without providing just compensation under the Constitution.
The Seventh Circuit upheld Chicago’s vehicle forfeiture scheme as consistent with the Fifth Amendment’s takings clause. The federal appeals court reasoned it is “an exercise of the city’s police power to enforce its traffic code.”
Sotomayor wrote: “I have serious concerns about that conclusion, which implicates a circuit split over whether, and under what circumstances, exercises of the state’s police power are immune to takings claims. Because that split would continue to benefit from further percolation, however, and because this case is not the best vehicle to resolve the split, I concur in the court’s denial of certiorari.”
Ryan O’Donnell and Michael Goree sued after the city impounded their vehicles.
O’Donnell said in his complaint he got two tickets for an expired meter and one for time-restricted parking, totaling about $524. When he couldn’t pay, the city impounded and sold his vehicle.
The city also took Goree’s vehicle and added tow and storage fees, even though he didn’t have outstanding fines. A co-signer on his vehicle faced about $560 in ticket debt from a different vehicle.
The city sold O’Donnell’s vehicle for its scrap value of $273 and gave Goree’s vehicle to the lienholder.
Neither petitioner received any compensation.
Meanwhile, Chicago generates roughly $264 million in traffic-ticket revenue and leads the nation in Chapter 13 bankruptcy filings, prompted in part by parking, traffic and vehicle compliance tickets.
“The result is devastating and counterproductive,” O’Donnell and Goree wrote in their petition. “The owner loses a car — usually their most important asset and only way to get to work, school, worship, etc. — and is left saddled not only with the existing ticket debt, but also new towing and storage fees. Often, drivers are left to pay off car loans on vehicles they no longer own.”
The Seventh Circuit rejected their argument that Chicago’s scheme is like the tax-forfeiture statute the high court invalidated in Tyler v. Hennepin County, for failure to return any surplus to the homeowner after a tax sale.
Instead, it compared the case to Bennis v. Michigan, where the justices held the government may seize property used in violation of a law without compensating the owner.
However, Sotomayor said the wrong precedent may have been applied: Unlike the laws discussed in Bennis, Chicago does not only impound vehicles involved in violations of its traffic code, such as in Goree’s case.
“Those features strongly suggest that ’the purpose of vehicle impoundments’ under Chicago’s scheme ‘is to collect a debt, not enforce public safety laws,’” the Barack Obama appointee wrote. “The city’s practice of surrendering cars to lienholders or selling them for their scrap value, rather than at a fair auction, only amplifies the potential constitutional infirmity.”
She encouraged courts to ensure that due deference to state police powers does not eclipse constitutional rights.

sources.news_title: Supreme Court won't revive 9/11 plea deal to end long-delayed prosecution
Supreme Court Rejects Khalid Sheik Mohammed's Plea
sources.text:
Supreme Court Rejects Khalid Sheik Mohammed’s Plea
The U.S. Supreme Court on October 19, 2026, denied a bid to revive a plea agreement for Khalid Sheik Mohammed. He is the accused mastermind of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.
The decision keeps the death penalty possible as the case heads toward a military trial scheduled for June 2028.
An earlier agreement would have allowed Mohammed to plead guilty. He would have been able to accept a sentence of life in prison instead of facing execution.
Former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin rejected the plea agreement in 2024. Austin ruled that the defense secretary had to approve such a major capital-punishment decision. A federal appeals court later upheld Austin’s authority to scrap the deal.
Mohammed remains detained at the Guantanamo Bay detention camp.
Khalid is accused of developing and directing the 2001 plot to hijack commercial airliners and crash them into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon, and a field in Pennsylvania.
In the 1990s, he participated in a plan to bomb 11 U.S.-bound transpacific airliners. He planned to target landmarks like the CIA headquarters and the Vatican.
He has been linked to other militant operations, including the 1993 World Trade Center bombing. He also directed the beheading of Wall Street Journal reporter Daniel Pearl.
Image: Wikimedia Commons

sources.news_title: US Supreme Court snubs bid to revive plea deal for accused 9/11 mastermind - THE LOCAL REPORT ARTICLES
sources.text:
The US Supreme Court declined on Monday to hear a bid by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the September 11, 2001, attacks, to revive a 2024 agreement that would have spared him the death penalty in exchange for a guilty plea — a deal scrapped by former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin.
The justices turned away appeals by Mohammed and two co-defendants who had also signed plea agreements of a lower court’s ruling that upheld Austin’s decision to void the deals. The US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit rejected an argument that Austin, who served under former President Joe Biden, had acted too late.
The Supreme Court’s action marks the latest milestone in a military prosecution of the detainees held in Guantanamo Bay, Cuba, that has been beset by two decades of legal gridlock.
In August, a US Air Force judge set the trial for Mohammed and his co-defendants for June 2028.
Mohammed remains the most well-known inmate at the Guantanamo detention facility, which was set up in 2002 by then-US President George W. Bush to house foreign terrorism suspects following the 9/11 attacks, which killed nearly 3,000 people. Mohammed is accused of orchestrating the plot to fly hijacked passenger jetliners into the World Trade Center in New York City and into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia.
The plea agreements for Mohammed and co-defendants Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid bin ‘Atash had been offered and accepted by the US official overseeing the Pentagon’s Guantanamo war court, prompting criticism by Republican lawmakers.
Austin revoked the deals two days later.
A military judge ruled that Austin lacked authority to invalidate the plea deals in a decision that was upheld in December by the US Court of Military Commission Review. The judge then scheduled prompt plea hearings.
The D.C. Circuit paused those proceedings, and in July 2025, a panel of that court — in a 2-1 vote — backed the decision to scrap the plea deals, saying that Austin “indisputably had legal authority to withdraw from the agreements.”
Defense attorneys for Mohammed and al Hawsawi, including lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union, urged the Supreme Court to hear the case. They said Austin’s action violated controlling military law and “prolonged the best chance for finality in the September 11 case in a quarter century.”
